body:
Found by my agent, but easy to understand. I think it's worth fixing (but I'm not sure yet what's the good fix)

----

### Describe the bug

A `prange` that holds the GIL hangs on GIL builds of Python when compiled with clang, as soon as the loop has a `lastprivate` variable. In practice that's every such loop, since the target always gets one. GCC and free-threaded builds are fine.

Clang adds a barrier at the end of a worksharing loop with `lastprivate`, even with `nowait`. That barrier runs right after the last iteration, so before the generated code reaches `PyEval_SaveThread()`. The thread that finishes first waits at this barrier with the GIL held, and the other threads wait for the GIL to run their first iteration.

### Code to reproduce the behaviour:

```cython
# cython: language_level=3, freethreading_compatible=True
from cython.parallel import prange

def run(int n=1000):
    cdef int i
    cdef int total = 0
    for i in prange(n, num_threads=4):
        total += 1
    return total
```

With conda-forge's `clang` and `llvm-openmp`:

```
CC=clang CFLAGS="-fopenmp -I$CONDA_PREFIX/include" \
    LDFLAGS="-fopenmp -L$CONDA_PREFIX/lib -Wl,-rpath,$CONDA_PREFIX/lib" cythonize -i repro.pyx
timeout 15 python -c "import repro; print(repro.run())"
```

| compiler | Python | Cython | 5 runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| clang 21.1 | 3.13 | 3.3.1 | 5 hangs |
| clang 14.0 | 3.13 | 3.3.1 | 5 hangs |
| clang 21.1 | 3.13 | master (7b3aab363) | 5 hangs |
| clang 21.1 | 3.14 | 3.3.1 | 5 hangs |
| clang 21.1 | 3.13 free-threaded | 3.3.1 | returns 1000 |
| GCC 15.3 | 3.13 | 3.3.1 | returns 1000 |

Backtrace with clang 21 and Python 3.13, trimmed. The main thread holds the GIL in the barrier, the 3 others are in the loop body:

```
Thread 4, 3, 2:
#6  take_gil (tstate=...) at Python/ceval_gil.c:341
#7  _PyEval_AcquireLock (tstate=...) at Python/ceval_gil.c
#8  _PyThreadState_Attach (tstate=...) at Python/pystate.c:2100
#9  PyEval_RestoreThread (tstate=...) at Python/ceval_gil.c:663
#10 __pyx_pf_5repro_run.omp_outlined_debug__ (...) at repro.c:2737   <- first statement of the loop body

Thread 1:
#5  __kmp_suspend_64<false, true>(int, kmp_flag_64<false, true>*) ()
#6  __kmp_wait_template<kmp_flag_64<false, true>, false, false, true>(...) ()
#7  __kmp_hyper_barrier_gather(...) ()
#8  __kmp_barrier_template<false>(...) ()
#9  __kmpc_barrier () from libomp.so
#10 __pyx_pf_5repro_run.omp_outlined_debug__ (...) at repro.c:2731   <- the "omp for" pragma
```

Clang reports all the barriers of the loop on the pragma line, so I checked the disassembly: the return address of thread 1 is right after the `__kmpc_barrier` call that follows `__kmpc_for_static_fini`, just before `PyEval_SaveThread`.

### Expected behaviour

`run()` returns 1000, as it does with GCC.

### OS

Linux (Ubuntu 24.04)

### Python version

3.13 and 3.14, GIL builds

### Cython version

3.3.1 and master

comment_data.body:
I would be moderately happy with generating an `#error` here with clang. Unless there's a _good_ fix then I think clang is just defective here and that failing to compile is the right thing to do (and certainly better than hanging at runtime).

I'd say this should happen even on freethreading builds because the GIL can end up enabled.
There's a bit of a gap here where we were skipping all OpenMP clang tests: see #8130. This should have been caught by our "sanitizers" tests which use clang on Linux.

> [...] as soon as the loop has a lastprivate variable. In practice that's every such loop, since the target always gets one

My current thought is to do better about identifying variables that are never used after the loop (which has to be a decent number of loop targets). That would let a good chunk of code work in clang (and the remainder could get an informative `#error`). I'll do this in the near future unless you tell me you have a better plan.

> My current thought is to do better about identifying variables that are never used after the loop (which has to be a decent number of loop targets). That would let a good chunk of code work in clang (and the remainder could get an informative #error). I'll do this in the near future unless you tell me you have a better plan.

I have a vibe-coded PR on my fork that is exactly doing that (https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/4). It removes the vast majority of real-world cases and reduces tremendously the number of barriers in the generated code for scikit-learn. I'm in the process of gaining a good enough understanding of it before opening it upstream.

I can continue that (I should be able to open it today or tomorrow), or if you want to take it over I'm happy with it (in which case I'll give a hand at reviewing the PR).

FYI, barrier counts in scikit-learn:

| Cython                       | GCC | clang 21  |
| ---------------------------- | --- | --------- |
| 3.3.1                        | 399 | 798       |
| #8121                | 465 | 798       |
| #8121 (explicit barrier version)  | 465 | 866 |
| #8121 + https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/4      | 67  | 69        |
| #8121 (explicit barrier) + https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/4 | 67  | 70  |
That's fine. I'll wait for your PR if you have something already.

Update:

https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/4 is quite brittle, things like aliasing make it hard to get right, and even harder to *prove* right. I'm trying to find other approaches.
Claude is not doing as well as it does on the kind of things I usually do (maybe just because of my own lack of expertise), it will take some time.

I'll try to have a look at that later too and see if I'd have done it very differently. It'd be worth saving the fragile cases if you still have them. 

If it's specifically the loop target, I wonder if it'd be possible to preserve it via a reduction instead? (That assumes that reductions don't also add a barrier)

The other thing that occurs to me as an option is to use the ompt tool callbacks to capture entering and exiting a barrier, and handle the GIL there. I'm not wildly happy with that since there looks to be one callback allowed per event type, so potentially Cython would be fighting other tools (and maybe even itself...). But it's an option that would hopefully be robust to however many barriers the compiler decides to add. (This is based on very little research so could well be a non-starter for reasons I don't know yet)
I think I have a substantially simpler plan here (although it'll have to be seen if it survives contact with reality...)

Ok, I'll let you try what you have in mind then, what I tried feels a bit too complex & brittle. Maybe https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/11 is the one worth opening (looks ok in terms of gain versus complexity), but I need to take a deeper look first.

Here is a summary of the attempts from my agent, in case it can help you:

-----

I have four PRs on my fork that remove the barriers that `firstprivate(x) lastprivate(x)` add to every `prange`: one at the start of the loop with GCC and clang, plus the end barrier with clang that causes this hang. **They're optimizations, not fixes**, but where a loop ends up with no `lastprivate`, clang has no end barrier left and the hang goes away. So they would leave the `#error` (or whatever handles the GIL at barriers) for fewer cases (and far fewer cases in practice I believe).

- [#4](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/4) uses `private(x)` when flow control proves that no read can tell the difference. That covers 398 of the 399 loops in scikit-learn. But the proof has to know every way `x` can be read, and these cases broke it during testing: `&s.a`, an array field used as a pointer, and a C++ reference argument. They're saved as tests in [#9](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/9) and [#11](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/11).
- [#9](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/9) keeps what both clauses mean, but does the copies by hand through temporaries, so it needs no clause and no barrier. Outside `parallel()` blocks, it needs no proof at all. Inside blocks, it needs an address check and complex code.
- [#10](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/10) tried to be a simpler [#4](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/4). Its first rule drops `firstprivate` when nothing in the body reads the value from before the loop. That turned out to be unsafe. When the last iteration doesn't assign `x`, `lastprivate` writes back an uninitialized value. In a block, the start barrier also kept the copy-out from racing with block code before the loop that reads `x`.
- [#11](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/11) is [#9](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/9) without the block part (+125/-4). A standalone `prange` copies by hand, with the same semantics and no barrier. Blocks keep today's clauses. In scikit-learn, that's 320 loops with no clause and 79 loops in blocks unchanged. It removes the hang for a standalone `prange` over numbers, pointers and C structs, which includes the repro above. C++ class variables and loops in blocks keep the clauses.

On the reduction idea for the target: its last value can be computed after the loop from the range, so it needs no clause at all. [#11](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/11) covers it with the other variables anyway.

*(Claude opinons)* https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/11 is the one I'd open here, on top of #8121. Blocks could get a follow-up later.

My proposed was essentially to always drop the `lastprivate` in favour of copying by hand and not to worry about `firstprivate` (so in principle a simpler version of your `#11`). Avoiding `firstprivate` is probably mostly an optimization, but I guess you're profiled it and it's worthwhile.

Looking at your proposed `#11` change the main bit that seems spurious to me is the `memcpy` and not copying C++ classes.  As far as I can tell, in C++ OpenMP will just call the copy constructor for `firstprivate` and the copy assignment operator (i.e. `out = loop_private;`) for `lastprivate` so I don't see the harm in doing that here too. With the proviso that it's probably easier to use the copy assignment operator for both.

> On the reduction idea for the target: its last value can be computed after the loop from the range[...]

In hindsight this (and the reduction) doesn't quite work in the general case because you can do e.g.

```
for x in prange(...):
    x = 5
```

For reference a simpler version which just avoids `lastprivate` and not `firstprivate` is https://github.com/da-woods/cython/pull/10. It passes the existing `prange` and `parallel` tests, and your tests (when I remove the ones for specific code generation)

I think advantages of your version are:
* the "copy variables outside loop" path is almost certainly worthwhile
* Avoiding `firstprivate` is probably worthwhile

The advantages of my version are:
* no restrictions on c++ classes (so just behaves close to how openmp does there)
* no restrictions on `prange` inside `parallel` so it doesn't need a fallback path where it sometimes adds `lastprivate`.

It's mainly presented so help you steal the two good bits.

Thanks!

> Avoiding `firstprivate` is probably worthwhile

In terms of performance, it has no impact for what I could measure.
But GCC warns "used uninitialized" on `firstprivate` alone for every variable not assigned before the loop, which includes most loop targets. I saw it on GCC 8, 11 and 15, and it gave 23 warnings on the [#11](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/11) test file against 0 today. Clang doesn't warn on these. That is what the memcpy helper in [#11](https://github.com/cakedev0/cython/pull/11) avoids.
Ah I see. I'd say "works with C++ classes" is probably more important that avoiding the warnings (although avoiding the warnings is a good thing if we can manage it)
Ok good to know thanks. Claude seems to really hate the warnings and try to avoid them at all cost, including over-killed brittle solutions 😅
FYI, I hope to go back at this in a week or two.

title: [BUG] prange holding the GIL hangs with clang: the end barrier from lastprivate runs with the GIL held
